body.heading: Roots meet fungi
paragraphs: Almost every tree in a forest has partners underground. Fungi called mycorrhizal fungi grow into and around the tree’s finest roots, extending them with a vast web of microscopic threads.

The trade is ancient and fair. The fungi are excellent at gathering water and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen from the soil, and they share them with the tree. In return, the tree pays in sugars made by photosynthesis — food the fungi cannot make themselves.

body.heading: Trading between trees
paragraphs: Because one fungus can connect to several trees at once, the threads form a network. Experiments using labelled carbon have shown that resources can move from tree to tree along these fungal pathways.

How much trading really happens in wild forests, and how much it matters, is something scientists are still actively debating. The network is real; the size of its role is the open question — and that is a normal, healthy state for a young field of science.

body.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Seen this way, a forest is not just a crowd of individual trees competing for light. It is also a community joined at the roots, with the soil as a shared marketplace.
It is one reason foresters and conservationists pay so much attention to soil. Damage the hidden network, and the visible forest suffers too.

takeaway: Beneath a forest, fungi and roots form a trading network — one reason a forest is more than the sum of its trees.
